title: Score-Calibrated Flow for Sampling from Unnormalized Densities with Applications to Generative Online Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: Score-Calibrated Flow for Sampling from Unnormalized Densities with Applications to Generative Online Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion and flow models provide expressive policy classes for online reinforcement learning (RL), enabling multimodal behaviors and improved performance. However, training these policies remains challenging: the critic specifies the desired policy as an unnormalized Boltzmann density but does not provide direct samples from it. Many existing methods rely on importance sampling to construct training signals, which can suffer from high variance, increasing computational cost and destabilizing training.
In this paper, we propose Score-Calibrated Flow (SCF), a simple and efficient algorithm for training generative models to sample from unnormalized densities without importance sampling or backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. Our key idea is to learn the desired flow by enforcing self-consistency, bypassing the challenging estimation of the target posterior mean. By jointly exploiting the prescribed target score and the structure of flow matching, we establish these self-consistency requirements as score-calibrated optimality conditions , first for the terminal density and then for the trainable velocity field. We prove that their unique solutions are, respectively, the target density and the ideal flow model that conditional flow matching (CFM) would recover if target samples were available.
We formulate the velocity condition as a fixed-point equation and exploit its conditional-expectation structure to construct a stop-gradient objective for enforcing it. The resulting training procedure retains the scalable sample–interpolate–regress structure of CFM despite the absence of target samples, using endpoints generated by the current flow. For online RL, the critic gradient supplies the target score at the generated actions, yielding a direct approach to actor training.
Experiments on RL benchmarks demonstrate that SCF matches or improves upon state-of-the-art generative-policy baselines, while substantially reducing training time.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and flow models learn expressive distributions by transforming initial noise through stochastic or deterministic dynamics ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) . They are appealing as policy classes since several distinct actions may be valuable in the same state, whereas a restrictive distribution may fail to represent these alternatives. Greater policy expressiveness can also translate into improved performance. These advantages have motivated the use of generative policies in imitation learning ( Chi et al., 2025 ) and offline reinforcement learning (RL) ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . In these settings, expert demonstrations or offline datasets provide the samples needed in the standard training recipe for generative models. In online RL, however, direct samples from the target density that policy improvement asks the actor to learn are unavailable. The difficulty is particularly clear in maximum-entropy RL ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) . At a given state s s , soft policy improvement targets the Boltzmann policy π Q ​ ( a | s ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( τ ​ Q ​ ( s , a ) ) \pi^{Q}(a|s)\propto\exp(\tau Q(s,a)) , where Q Q is the critic and τ > 0 \tau>0 is the inverse temperature. Soft actor-critic (SAC) approximates this target within a Gaussian policy family using a mode-seeking objective. A diffusion or flow policy offers a richer representation, but standard training methods such as conditional flow matching (CFM) require samples from the Boltzmann policy, whereas the critic provides only evaluations of Q ⁡ ( s , a ) Q(s,a) and its action gradient ∇ a Q ​ ( s , a ) \nabla_{a}Q(s,a) . More broadly, the challenge is learning to sample from unnormalized densities , rather than learning from target samples as in standard generative training. Existing methods for generative online RL can be grouped into four categories (see Appendix A for a detailed discussion). Direct backpropagation ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Lyu et al., 2025 ; Celik et al., 2025 ) optimizes critic-based objectives by differentiating through the entire sampling trajectory, which incurs substantial computational cost and destabilizes training. Value-guided sampling ( Psenka et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) uses critic information to guide sampling and exploration through stochastic or deterministic dynamics. Weighted regression ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) trains the policy on candidate actions using value-dependent weights, adding sampling overhead and making the training target depend on the proposal distribution and weighting rule. These approaches rely on surrogate objectives or sampling approximations that can introduce bias relative to exact soft policy improvement. In contrast, Boltzmann targeting ( Dong et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Jain et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) derives training signals directly from the Boltzmann density, recovering the desired policy at the ideal population optimum. In practice, however, the required posterior means are typically estimated through multi-particle importance sampling. This incurs computational overhead at each update and can produce high-variance estimates that destabilize training. In this paper, we propose Score-Calibrated Flow (SCF), a simple and efficient algorithm for learning to sample from unnormalized densities. Our key idea is to learn the desired flow by enforcing self-consistency, bypassing the challenging estimation of the target posterior mean. By jointly exploiting the prescribed target score and the structure of flow matching, we establish these self-consistency requirements as score-calibrated optimality conditions . We first derive conditions that characterize the target density, then develop corresponding conditions for the trainable velocity field. The velocity condition takes the form of a fixed-point equation whose conditional-expectation structure enables training with self-generated samples. Specifically, SCF generates an endpoint with the current flow, interpolates it with independent source noise, and constructs a regression target whose conditional mean equals the right-hand side of the fixed-point equation. This retains the scalable sample–interpolate–regress structure of CFM despite the absence of target samples, without importance sampling or backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. Our contributions are summarized as follows. 1. Score-calibrated optimality conditions. We establish necessary and sufficient self-consistency conditions for both the terminal density and the trainable velocity field. Their unique solutions are, respectively, the target density and the ideal flow model that CFM would recover if target samples were available. 2. Scalable training from self-generated samples. We construct a sample-wise regression target whose conditional mean equals the score-calibration operator applied to the current velocity. We use this target in a stop-gradient objective to enforce the velocity condition. Each target requires only one self-generated endpoint and one target-score evaluation, avoiding importance sampling and backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. 3. Principled design and strong RL performance. We derive coefficient schedules that cancel source-end singular factors and handle bounded actions through an exact change of variables that preserves the intended target density. Experiments on online RL benchmarks demonstrate that SCF matches or improves upon state-of-the-art generative-policy baselines, with substantial savings in training time.

sections.heading: 3 Score-Calibrated Flow
sections.text: In this section, we develop Score-Calibrated Flow (SCF) for learning generative models to sample from unnormalized densities. The key paradigm shift enabling SCF is to reinterpret the flow matching framework as a one-to-one correspondence between terminal densities and their associated ideal flow models, rather than solely as a procedure for learning from target samples. Each terminal density determines the population minimizer of the CFM loss, which is the velocity field that CFM would learn if samples from that density were available. Conversely, pushing the source density through the resulting flow induces the terminal density. We exploit the two directions of this correspondence to develop our optimality conditions. First, we view the flow model as a function of its terminal density and derive a score-calibrated condition that characterizes the target density through the flow it induces. We then let the trainable velocity field determine its own terminal density through the pushforward map, yielding a self-consistency condition directly on the velocity. This condition takes the form of a fixed-point equation whose conditional-expectation structure enables scalable regression using self-generated samples. Finally, we develop principled design choices to address practical challenges, including numerical singularities and bounded domains, and demonstrate how to apply SCF to generative online RL.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we proposed Score-Calibrated Flow (SCF), a simple and efficient method for learning to sample from unnormalized densities with applications to generative online RL. By shifting from target posterior-mean estimation to self-consistency enforcement, we derived score-calibrated optimality conditions for both terminal densities and velocity fields. Their conditional-expectation structure yields a stop-gradient regression objective using self-generated samples. Experiments demonstrated strong performance and computational efficiency of SCF.

sections.heading: A.1 Generative Online Reinforcement Learning
sections.text: We organize existing methods by how they construct supervision signals for actor training.

sections.heading: Direct backpropagation.
sections.text: DACER ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , FlowRL ( Lyu et al., 2025 ) , and DIME ( Celik et al., 2025 ) differentiate critic-based objectives through the sampling trajectory, incorporating additional approximations and regularization to make policy optimization more stable. Specifically, DACER estimates policy entropy by fitting Gaussian mixture models to sampled actions, FlowRL uses a flow-matching surrogate for Wasserstein regularization toward high-value replay-buffer behaviors, and DIME optimizes a tractable lower bound on the maximum-entropy objective. Despite these measures, backpropagation through the full sampling trajectory incurs substantial computational and memory costs and poses a nonnegligible risk of training instability.

sections.heading: Value-guided sampling.
sections.text: QSM ( Psenka et al., 2024 ) trains a diffusion score network using critic gradients at noisy actions, while QFlex ( Wei et al., 2026 ) performs critic-gradient ascent from a learned source and fits a flow model to the resulting endpoints. Unlike our method, QSM and QFlex do not establish an exact characterization that uniquely identifies both the prescribed Boltzmann density and its velocity from CFM construction. Their guidance relies on repeated action-refinement steps, and evaluating the critic at noisy actions can expose it to inputs where its estimates are unreliable. We instead derive regression targets from score-calibrated optimality conditions and evaluate the critic gradient at clean actions. Each target requires only one endpoint-score evaluation, and the continuous-time formulation is independent of the number of sampling steps, without requiring an additional multi-step guidance procedure.

sections.heading: Weighted regression.
sections.text: QVPO ( Ding et al., 2024 ) trains a diffusion policy with Q-dependent weights and entropy regularization. Related approaches include reward-weighted flow matching ( Fan et al., 2025 ) and diffusion policy mirror descent ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . These methods use importance sampling to construct weighted regression objectives and therefore remain susceptible to high-variance training signals when the importance weights become concentrated. Generating and evaluating multiple candidate actions further increases computational cost. Moreover, their induced training densities depend on the proposal distribution and weighting rule and generally differ from the prescribed Boltzmann target π Q \pi^{Q} , so even exact optimization may not recover the desired policy.

sections.heading: Boltzmann targeting.
sections.text: MaxEntDP ( Dong et al., 2025 ) and SDAC ( Ma et al., 2025 ) use Q-weighted noise signals to train noise-prediction and score networks, respectively. DQS ( Jain et al., 2025 ) adapts iterated denoising energy matching ( Akhound-Sadegh et al., 2024 ) to train a score network using Q-weighted averages of critic gradients. RFM ( Li et al., 2026 ) identifies these noise-expectation and gradient-expectation methods as instances of a shared posterior-mean estimation problem, and provides a principled way to combine both families through Stein control variates for variance reduction. These formulations target the Boltzmann density at the ideal population optimum, but their practical estimators rely on importance sampling, incurring computational overhead and estimator variance. SCF instead enforces score-calibrated self-consistency through regression on self-generated endpoints, without explicitly estimating the target posterior mean.

sections.heading: A.2 Learning to Sample from Unnormalized Densities
sections.text: Learning generative samplers from unnormalized densities has been extensively studied, with representative approaches based on normalizing flows ( Noé et al., 2019 ; Papamakarios et al., 2021 ) and diffusion models ( Zhang and Chen, 2022 ; Vargas et al., 2023 ; Akhound-Sadegh et al., 2024 ) . We focus on recent matching-based methods that avoid both importance-weighted training targets and backpropagation through sampling trajectories. Adjoint Sampling (AS) ( Havens et al., 2025 ) derives an endpoint-gradient regression objective from stochastic optimal control. Adjoint Schrödinger Bridge Sampler (ASBS) ( Liu et al., 2025 ) extends this construction beyond memoryless reference processes by alternating between learning a diffusion drift and a terminal corrector. Bridge Matching Sampler (BMS) ( Blessing et al., 2026 ) derives diffusion-matching targets from a fixed-point iteration perspective. Flow Sampling (FS) ( Havens et al., 2026 ) constructs regression targets by combining the conditional velocity with an endpoint-score correction. SCF grounds its training rule in optimality conditions that uniquely characterize the target density and ideal flow velocity under mild regularity requirements. BMS and FS adopt a fixed-point iteration perspective on training with self-generated samples, but do not establish that the desired sampler is the unique fixed point ( Blessing et al., 2026 ; Havens et al., 2026 ) . AS establishes fixed-point uniqueness only under the additional assumption of reciprocal-projection invariance ( Havens et al., 2025 ) . This is closer in spirit to our density optimality condition, where the flow is prescribed by the candidate density. Our velocity optimality condition goes further: it rules out spurious fixed points without presupposing a density–flow consistency. ASBS establishes convergence of its alternating updates under the assumption that each stage reaches its critical point, but does not establish uniqueness of the joint critical points of its coupled drift–corrector matching equations ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . SCF instead derives necessary and sufficient conditions directly for the terminal density and trainable velocity. Their unique solutions are the target density π \pi and the ideal velocity v π v^{\pi} that CFM would learn from target samples. Moreover, the four methods above learn the drifts of stochastic differential equations (SDEs). Their sampling procedures rely on stochastic simulation, which may require a large number of function evaluations (NFEs), increasing computational costs during both training and inference. FS illustrates a structural limitation of this formulation: its target-score correction is proportional to the squared diffusion coefficient, so setting this coefficient to zero eliminates explicit target-score supervision ( Havens et al., 2026 ) . The remaining objective reduces to CFM on self-generated endpoints, which reproduces the current density without identifying the prescribed target. Thus, simply removing the diffusion noise does not yield a training objective that ensures the learned velocity field generates the prescribed target density through ODE sampling. In contrast, SCF derives its velocity regression objective from score-calibrated optimality conditions, retaining target-score supervision without relying on stochastic sampling dynamics.

sections.text: We evaluate 20 20 checkpoints per run, evenly spaced in model updates, each with 5 × 10 4 5\times 10^{4} generated samples. The checkpoint with the smallest W 2 W_{2} is selected and re-evaluated on fresh generated and reference samples, and we report the mean and standard deviation of the resulting values over five seeds. • Mode total variation distance (mode TVD). Each generated sample is assigned to the component with the nearest mean, and w ^ k \widehat{w}_{k} denotes the fraction of samples assigned to component k k . The mode TVD 1 2 ​ ∑ k = 0 7 | w ^ k − 1 8 | \frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=0}^{7}\left|\widehat{w}_{k}-\tfrac{1}{8}\right| measures how evenly the eight modes are covered. • 2 2 -Wasserstein distance ( W 2 W_{2} ). Computed exactly under the squared Euclidean cost between 2000 2000 generated samples and 2000 2000 target samples; we repeat the computation 20 20 times with nonoverlapping subsets of generated samples and fresh target samples, and report the median. As a finite-sample estimate it does not vanish even for perfect samples: between two independent sets of target samples it equals 0.719 0.719 , which serves as the reference floor.

sections.heading: Shared settings.
sections.text: For each set of RL tasks, all algorithms are integrated into one JAX codebase and share the training loop, replay buffer, networks, and optimizer, summarized in Table 1 , to ensure a fair comparison. On the DeepMind Control Suite we build on the codebase of RFM ( Li et al., 2026 ) ( https://github.com/azizanlab/ReverseFlowMatching ); on HumanoidBench we build on the codebase of QFlex ( Wei et al., 2026 ) ( https://github.com/LNSGroup/Qflex ). Each algorithm is implemented following its open-source implementation. All training and evaluation runs are conducted on a desktop with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU and an Intel Core Ultra 9 285K CPU.

sections.heading: Appendix D Ablation Studies
sections.text: In this section, we analyze how different design choices affect the performance of SCF. We conduct the experiments on the h1-run task from HumanoidBench. All variants follow the settings of Appendix C.2 and are trained with five seeds; the training curves are shown in Figure 4 . First, we vary the NFEs used to sample actions during both training and evaluation. SCF uses 10 10 NFEs by default; we compare with 6 6 and 20 20 NFEs. As shown in Figure 4 (left), the three settings perform similarly, indicating that the algorithm is robust to the choice of NFEs. Second, we study the coefficient choices in the regression target ( 18 ). Our default choice ( 44 ) combines the conditional velocity, current velocity, and score-based term, with λ t = η ​ α t 2 \lambda_{t}=\eta\alpha_{t}^{2} canceling the inverse powers of α t \alpha_{t} in the score-based contribution (Proposition B.6 ). As an ablation, we set λ t = 1 \lambda_{t}=1 and ζ t = 0 \zeta_{t}=0 , leaving only the score-based term. Since this term is unbounded as t → 0 t\to 0 , we sample t t uniformly from [ 0.05 , 1 ] [0.05,1] to avoid the singularity. Nevertheless, this variant fails to learn: for every seed, the regression loss exceeds 10 24 10^{24} within the first 2 × 10 6 2\times 10^{6} environment steps, and the return never improves (Figure 4 , right). These results confirm that the singularity cancellation developed in Appendix B.4 is both theoretically well motivated and practically essential for stable training.

However, training these policies remains challenging: the critic specifies the desired policy as an unnormalized Boltzmann density but does not provide direct samples from it. Many existing methods rely on importance sampling to construct training signals, which can suffer from high variance, increasing computational cost and destabilizing training. In this paper, we propose Score-Calibrated Flow (SCF), a simple and efficient algorithm for training generative models to sample from unnormalized densities without importance sampling or backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. Our key idea is to learn the desired flow by enforcing self-consistency, bypassing the challenging estimation of the target posterior mean. By jointly exploiting the prescribed target score and the structure of flow matching, we establish these self-consistency requirements as score-calibrated optimality conditions , first for the terminal density and then for the trainable velocity field. We prove that their unique solutions are, respectively, the target density and the ideal flow model that conditional flow matching (CFM) would recover if target samples were available. We formulate the velocity condition as a fixed-point equation and exploit its conditional-expectation structure to construct a stop-gradient objective for enforcing it. The resulting training procedure retains the scalable sample–interpolate–regress structure of CFM despite the absence of target samples, using endpoints generated by the current flow. For online RL, the critic gradient supplies the target score at the generated actions, yielding a direct approach to actor training. Experiments on RL benchmarks demonstrate that SCF matches or improves upon state-of-the-art generative-policy baselines, while substantially reducing training time. † † footnotetext: Correspondence to Zeyang Li ( zeyang@mit.edu ) and Yunan Wang ( wangyn25@mit.edu ). 1 Introduction Diffusion and flow models learn expressive distributions by transforming initial noise through stochastic or deterministic dynamics ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) . They are appealing as policy classes since several distinct actions may be valuable in the same state, whereas a restrictive distribution may fail to represent these alternatives. Greater policy expressiveness can also translate into improved performance. These advantages have motivated the use of generative policies in imitation learning ( Chi et al., 2025 ) and offline reinforcement learning (RL) ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . In these settings, expert demonstrations or offline datasets provide the samples needed in the standard training recipe for generative models. In online RL, however, direct samples from the target density that policy improvement asks the actor to learn are unavailable. The difficulty is particularly clear in maximum-entropy RL ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) . At a given state s s , soft policy improvement targets the Boltzmann policy π Q ​ ( a | s ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( τ ​ Q ​ ( s , a ) ) \pi^{Q}(a|s)\propto\exp(	au Q(s,a)) , where Q Q is the critic and τ > 0 	au>0 is the inverse temperature. Soft actor-critic (SAC) approximates this target within a Gaussian policy family using a mode-seeking objective. A diffusion or flow policy offers a richer representation, but standard training methods such as conditional flow matching (CFM) require samples from the Boltzmann policy, whereas the critic provides only evaluations of Q ⁡ ( s , a ) Q(s,a) and its action gradient ∇ a Q ​ ( s , a )

Existing methods for generative online RL can be grouped into four categories (see Appendix A for a detailed discussion). Direct backpropagation ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Lyu et al., 2025 ; Celik et al., 2025 ) optimizes critic-based objectives by differentiating through the entire sampling trajectory, which incurs substantial computational cost and destabilizes training. Value-guided sampling ( Psenka et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) uses critic information to guide sampling and exploration through stochastic or deterministic dynamics. Weighted regression ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) trains the policy on candidate actions using value-dependent weights, adding sampling overhead and making the training target depend on the proposal distribution and weighting rule. These approaches rely on surrogate objectives or sampling approximations that can introduce bias relative to exact soft policy improvement. In contrast, Boltzmann targeting ( Dong et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Jain et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) derives training signals directly from the Boltzmann density, recovering the desired policy at the ideal population optimum. In practice, however, the required posterior means are typically estimated through multi-particle importance sampling. This incurs computational overhead at each update and can produce high-variance estimates that destabilize training. In this paper, we propose Score-Calibrated Flow (SCF), a simple and efficient algorithm for learning to sample from unnormalized densities. Our key idea is to learn the desired flow by enforcing self-consistency, bypassing the challenging estimation of the target posterior mean. By jointly exploiting the prescribed target score and the structure of flow matching, we establish these self-consistency requirements as score-calibrated optimality conditions . We first derive conditions that characterize the target density, then develop corresponding conditions for the trainable velocity field. The velocity condition takes the form of a fixed-point equation whose conditional-expectation structure enables training with self-generated samples. Specifically, SCF generates an endpoint with the current flow, interpolates it with independent source noise, and constructs a regression target whose conditional mean equals the right-hand side of the fixed-point equation. This retains the scalable sample–interpolate–regress structure of CFM despite the absence of target samples, without importance sampling or backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. We construct a sample-wise regression target whose conditional mean equals the score-calibration operator applied to the current velocity. We use this target in a stop-gradient objective to enforce the velocity condition. Each target requires only one self-generated endpoint and one target-score evaluation, avoiding importance sampling and backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. 3. Principled design and strong RL performance. We derive coefficient schedules that cancel source-end singular factors and handle bounded actions through an exact change of variables that preserves the intended target density. The key paradigm shift enabling SCF is to reinterpret the flow matching framework as a one-to-one correspondence between terminal densities and their associated ideal flow models, rather than solely as a procedure for learning from target samples. Each terminal density determines the population minimizer of the CFM loss, which is the velocity field that CFM would learn if samples from that density were available.
